newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Doleful Australian dlr finds size does matter.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Doleful Australian dlr finds size does matter.

text.p: The Australian dollar subsided to its lowest local finish since mid-August on Tuesday as a jaded market counted down the last hours to a long-anticipated decision on domestic interest rates.

The policy making board of the Reserve Bank held its monthly meeting today and analysts firmly believed it had sanctioned a 0.50 point cut in official cash rates to 6.5 percent, probably to be announced Wednesday morning.
The market had discounted such a move for weeks, giving the dollar a certain amount of immunity, but dealers were concerned the cut would be more sizeable, and so seriously test support.

By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local dollar had drooped to US$0.7861/66 from an early US$0.7875/80 and US$0.7883/88 late here Monday. That was its lowest local finish since August 16 and only just above its intra-day trough of US$0.7855.
Traders said support had been solid there so far with exporters and Japanese investors on the bid, but would not last last long if the RBA did indeed ease by more than 0.5 point.

It also eased on most crosses, losing large chunks of ground to the Canadian and New Zealand dollars. Dealers said offshore investors viewed these as close competitors to the A$ and the threat of a rate cut had them switching funds in their favour.
The local currency did hold its nerve against the yen thanks to a rally in US$/yen and expectations the recent burst of yen/A$ dual currency samurai demand would continue this week.
It stood at 89.44/54 in late trade from 89.20/30 Monday and that helped the trade weighted index finish unchanged at 58.2.
At the moment the currency's yield premium was still meaty enough to attract Japanese funds, but dealers feared it could thin to unappetising levels if the RBA took a cleaver to rates.
Thus a cut of 75 basis points or more was expected to see US$0.7850/55 support sundered with ease and have the dollar threatening the pivotal US$0.7810 level before day's end.
Conversely, an easing of only 0.5 point would now prove a relief to dollar bulls and actually see the currency bounce to last week's top around US$0.7940.

And no move at all would be taken as a sign an easing was off the agenda until enterprise wage data were released in late November, which would likely trigger a wave of short covering taking the dollar to October's US$0.7985 high. Most, however, felt it would only clear 80 cents if the RBA raised rates.
The central bank's decision should be known, one way or the other, by 9.30 am (2230 GMT) -- the usual time for policy announcements -- on Wednesday morning.

Ironically, the preoccupation with monetary policy has actually served to insulate the dollar from the recent slide in commodity prices. The collpase continued Monday with the Commodity Research Bureau index off 0.78 point to 236.52, its lowest finish since August last year.
The fall wiped out all the gains made this year -- the index reached a high of 263.79 in April -- which at the time was cited as a major reason for the dollar's rally from 73 cents.
Once the cut was out, the way the market might even re-focus on this weakness, with negative implications for the dollar.
